evals.prompt: We ingest 500 million 8 KB JSON telemetry files (~4 TB total raw size) every week into an S3 bucket in ap-south-1, and we delete them after 7 days. To slash our storage bill, our developer wants to add an S3 Lifecycle rule on Day 0 that immediately transitions all 500 million 8 KB files to either **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** or **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** before deleting them on Day 7. Why is this a disastrous FinOps anti-pattern, and what architecture should we use instead?
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-storage skill and flags all three small-object and short-retention cost traps: (1) S3 Intelligent-Tiering **never auto-tiers objects smaller than `128 KB`** (they remain permanently billed at the Frequent Access tier rate), (2) S3 Standard-IA/One Zone-IA/Glacier Instant Retrieval enforce a **`128 KB` minimum billable object size** (inflating 8 KB objects by 16x) while Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive add **`40 KB` per-object metadata overhead** plus massive per-1,000 Lifecycle transition `PUT` fees across 500 million objects, and (3) deleting objects on Day 7 triggers early-deletion penalties for the full **`90-day` (Glacier Instant/Flexible) or `180-day` (Glacier Deep Archive) minimum storage duration**; recommends keeping 7-day ephemeral data in `S3 Standard` with a 7-day `Expiration` rule and compacting small JSON files via Firehose/Glue into larger **Apache Parquet** objects or **Amazon S3 Tables (Apache Iceberg)**.
expectations: Activates the aws-storage skill and explains that S3 Intelligent-Tiering never transitions objects smaller than 128 KB to Infrequent Access or Archive tiers (keeping them billed at Frequent Access rates)

Explains the small-object and minimum-duration penalties: 128 KB minimum billable size on IA/Glacier Instant (16x inflation for 8 KB files), 40 KB per-object metadata + 500M transition request charges on Glacier, and 30-day (IA) / 90-day (Glacier) / 180-day (Deep Archive) minimum storage duration charges when deleting at 7 days
Recommends keeping 7-day short-lived data in S3 Standard with a direct Lifecycle Expiration rule and compacting small JSON events into larger Parquet files or Amazon S3 Tables (Apache Iceberg)

evals.prompt: We want 4 EC2 application servers in ap-south-1a to simultaneously read and write shared customer PDF uploads. To avoid managing NFS, we plan to create an `io2` EBS volume with `MultiAttachEnabled: true`, format it with standard `xfs` (or `ext4`), and mount it read/write on all 4 EC2 instances at `/var/uploads`. Will this work safely?
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-storage skill, explicitly warns against mounting an `xfs` or `ext4` EBS Multi-Attach volume read/write across multiple EC2 instances because standard Linux/Windows filesystems (`xfs`, `ext4`, `NTFS`) are **not cluster-aware** and do not coordinate block locks or kernel page caches across hosts, which causes **immediate filesystem corruption and silent data loss**; explains that EBS Multi-Attach (`io1`/`io2`, single-AZ up to 16 Nitro instances) requires either a cluster-aware filesystem (`GFS2`, `OCFS2`) or raw block I/O fencing (such as Oracle RAC), and recommends **Amazon EFS** or **Amazon FSx (OpenZFS / NetApp ONTAP)** (or direct S3 object storage) for shared file access across multiple instances.
expectations: Activates the aws-storage skill and explicitly warns that mounting an `xfs` or `ext4` EBS Multi-Attach volume read/write across multiple EC2 instances causes immediate filesystem corruption and data loss

Explains why: standard filesystems (`xfs`, `ext4`) are not cluster-aware and lack distributed lock and page-cache coordination, whereas EBS Multi-Attach (`io1`/`io2`, up to 16 Nitro instances in a single AZ) requires a cluster-aware filesystem (`GFS2`, `OCFS2`) or application-level block fencing
Recommends managed shared file storage (Amazon EFS or Amazon FSx for OpenZFS / NetApp ONTAP) or Amazon S3 for shared multi-instance file access

Recommends routing cross-VPC and on-premises Multi-AZ ONTAP NFS/SMB traffic through AWS Transit Gateway, while noting why Single-AZ ONTAP and iSCSI/intercluster endpoints work over VPC Peering (they use secondary IPs within the VPC CIDR)

evals.prompt: Help us resolve two FSx operational issues in ap-south-1: (1) On **Amazon FSx for OpenZFS**, `DeleteSnapshot` fails on last week's snapshot, and switching a volume's compression setting from `NONE` to `ZSTD` didn't reduce the space used by existing files; (2) On **Amazon FSx for Windows File Server**, a team used `robocopy` to migrate a deduplicated on-premises Windows share and corrupted files, and now wants to shrink the FSx for Windows file system from 10 TiB down to 4 TiB in place.
evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-storage skill and resolves both sets of issues: (1) On **FSx for OpenZFS**, a snapshot **cannot be deleted while a dependent writable clone volume still exists** (delete the dependent clone first), and ZFS compression changes (`ZSTD`/`LZ4`) are **not retroactive** — they apply only to newly written blocks unless existing data is copied/rewritten; and (2) On **FSx for Windows File Server**, careless `robocopy` flags corrupt Windows NTFS deduplication reparse points (recommend **AWS DataSync** to preserve NTFS ACLs, SACLs, and deduplicated files with checksum validation), and FSx for Windows storage capacity is **increase-only** (it cannot be shrunk in place; shrinking requires creating a new smaller file system and migrating via AWS DataSync).
expectations: Activates the aws-storage skill and explains that an FSx for OpenZFS snapshot cannot be deleted (`DeleteSnapshot`) while a dependent writable clone volume exists, and that ZSTD/LZ4 compression changes apply only to newly written data unless existing files are rewritten

Explains that migrating deduplicated Windows shares with `robocopy` can corrupt NTFS deduplication reparse points and recommends AWS DataSync to preserve NTFS ACLs/SACLs with end-to-end checksum verification
States that FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity is increase-only and cannot be shrunk in place (requiring a new smaller file system + AWS DataSync migration)

evals.prompt: Our analytics and legacy Linux apps in ap-south-1 need file-style access to objects in an S3 General Purpose bucket, and our engineers are confused between **Amazon S3 Files**, **Mountpoint for Amazon S3**, and **AWS Storage Gateway (S3 File Gateway)**. evals.expected_output: Activates the aws-storage skill and contrasts all three: (1) **Amazon S3 Files** (`mount -t s3files`, cloud-native Multi-AZ NFSv4.1/v4.2 shared file system built on EFS infrastructure for EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda/Fargate with full POSIX permissions, file locking, small-file caching, large-read streaming from S3, and automatic ~60-second bidirectional sync where S3 is the system of record and concurrent edit conflicts move the NFS version to `.s3files-lost+found-{fs-id}`), (2) **Mountpoint for Amazon S3** (host-local high-throughput FUSE client on EC2/EKS/ECS optimized for read-heavy and sequential new-object writes without full POSIX random overwrite, locking, or directory rename semantics), and (3) **AWS Storage Gateway — S3 File Gateway** (on-premises VM/hardware appliance with a local SSD cache exposing S3 over NFS/SMB to on-premises clients).

Contrasts Mountpoint for Amazon S3 as a local FUSE client for high-throughput sequential reads and new-file writes (lacking full POSIX in-place file modification, locking, or cheap directory renames)
Contrasts AWS Storage Gateway (S3 File Gateway) as a hybrid on-premises appliance with a local cache for on-premises NFS/SMB clients
